messages.subject: Strange traceplots
parts:
Hi all!

First of all, thank you for this amazing group!

I wanted to share with you some traceplots that I get for two parameters (transition probabilities) in a multievent capture recapture model. I wonder if you could help me understanding what is the meaning or the cause behind them.

I have spent a while learning and building multievent models to examine differences in survival in relation with breeding status in a wild bird.

We analyzed the recapture histories of 983 birds along 10 capture occassions (2012-2021). Due to the differences in the way of marking the birds along the years, we decided to simplify our dataset and keep individuals that have been marked the same way (individuals born in 2011, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020). This provokes that during the time lapse between 2012 and 2016, we are only following birds born in 2011. I mean, there is not entry of new individuals in the capture histories until 2016, so the number of birds descends rapidly. In this model, we are not including an age effect.


For this model we calculated different parameters:

Some of them varying with time, sex and breeding status:
Survival probability:
  1. phiBreedersMales
  2. phiBreedersFemales
  3. phiFloatersMales
  4. phiFloatersFemales
Transition probability between states, also varying with time, sex and breeding status:
  1. psiBreedersMales (this would represent the probability of changing status from breeder to floater in males)
  2. psiBreedersFemales (this would represent the probability of changing status from breeder to floater in females)
  3. psiFloatersMales (this would represent the probability of changing status from  floater to breeder in males)
  4. psiFloatersFemales( (this would represent the probability of changing status from  floater to breeder in females)
Recapture probability constant over time but dependent on sex and breeding status.
  1. pBreedersMales
  2. pBreedersFemales
  3. pFloatersMales
  4. pFloatersFemales
All works perfectly in this model, chains converge and mix well for all parameters  but for the transition probabilities of male and female breeders (transition from breeder -> floater)

I get the following traceplots:



We are trying to understand why there is like a multimodal traceplot in the case of males. We don't know if it has to do to the few amount of data in some years or to the fact that the number of transitions from breeder to floater is actually very low in our population (we know this from our longitudinal dataset). In the case of the traceplots for transition probability from floater to breeder, they look good, with a high number of n.eff and a R-hat = 1.

Any thoughts? We have tried to run longer chainsand change the priors. But with had no ''luck''. The traceplots keep looking the same.  When we set these transition probabilities as constants overtime and only dependent of breeding status and sex, traceplots are good!

Sorry if I didn't explain myselft well!

And thank you!!

messages.author: 73b37a8108370eea
messages.subject: Re: Strange traceplots
parts:
Hello Iraida,

Have you estimted these parameters on the logit or real scale? I have a feeling that since your estimates are close to zero (but bounded at 0), and that those estimates for males are relatively variable (in which case you might be right, the low sample size could be playing a role here), there might be a lot of samples accumulating near the boundary, which could potentially create the weird bi-modal pattern you're seeing. If you estimated these parameters on the real scale, do you get the same patterns? If you have a beta_psi_male[T] somewhere  in your code, it might be interesting to see what that traceplot looks like since it won't be bounded at 0.

If you do not have that, you could estimate a beta_psi_male on the real scale using a vague normal prior (and removing any priors for psi on the [0,1] scale) and adding a link between your beta and actual psi, maybe something like

#prior
beta_psi_male ~ dnorm(0, sd=1.5)

for (T in n.occ){
logit(psi_male[T]) <- beta_psi_male[T]
[rest of meaningful code here where you can use psi_male[T] the way you did before...]
}

Hard to go much further without the code though.

It's just a hunch and I might be wrong, but knowing what's going on with your parameters on the [-Inf, +Inf] scale might help you diagnose what's going on.

Hope this helps,

Fred L

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: Strange traceplots
parts:
Hi Iraida

Following on from the answer of Fred. You may be interested in the new package nimbleNoBounds  which provides a set of transformed distributions with exactly this in mind.  In your case I would expect that using this package could help increase the effective sample size. However, I'm not optimistic that it would remove the bi-modality in your case. 

Concerning multi-modal posteriors, the package nimbleAPT has been designed to provide more efficient sampling (i.e. increased frequency of between-mode jumps, thus higher effective sample size). That said, it is unclear whether or not this would provide a significant improvement in efficiency in your case, because the multiple modes are not separated by low probability zones - on the flip side, their variances are very different - so perhaps the extra effort can be worth it.  

Concerning the interpretation of the multi-modality... that's hard to answer, although it often arises in ecological models. Perhaps you could try to dissect which elements of the data set are fitted well under low and high values of psi_maleT[3]. One approach would be to look at the LogProbs of various data nodes under low and high values of psi_maleT[3] and try to identify what (if anything) changes when switching from the low mode to the high mode. Alternatively (and probably simpler), for whatever plots you're generating from the model output, you could use two different colours for representing low and high modes of psi_maleT[3] respectively. 

Best regards
David

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Strange traceplots
parts:
Hi David (and Iraida),

I hope Iraida doesn't mind that I share this, but off-list I suggested she parameterize the temporal random effects as non-centered. This made the multimodality go away. The likely cause of it was that samplers were getting stuck to low mu and high sigma values, leading to the multimodal traceplots.

Kind regards,

Matt

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: Strange traceplots
parts:
Just following up with a comparison between the prior proposed by Fred and one that is available in nimbleNoBounds.

library(nimbleNoBounds)
x = rnorm(n=1e5, 0, sd=1.5)
y = ilogit(x)
par(mfrow=n2mfrow(2))
hist(x, n=101, freq=FALSE)
curve(dLogitBeta(x, 1, 1), -7, 7, n=1001, col="red", add=TRUE)
hist(y, n=101, freq=FALSE)
curve(dbeta(x, 1, 1), 0, 1, n=1001, col="red", add=TRUE)

 I've attached a pdf with the output from this code chunk. 

Best regards
David
